author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: see supply, play supply, and measure what pacing means (rules/save 29)
body:
Supply has governed every campaign since rules 27 and could not be seen. The
ground a realm's hearths and depots can feed is now outlined under everything
else on the map, on by default and switchable from the map guide. The
observation carries the same reach that already answers each army's supply
status, computed once rather than twice, so the overlay costs nothing new.

Rules 28 also let a realm create an upkeep obligation with no way to end it short
of an enemy taking the depot - a flaw introduced in that slice. A realm may now
pull down its own depot from the company standing on it.

The AI plays supply. A realm at war whose force is wasting outside supply raises
a depot under it rather than abandon the operation: one a turn, out of surplus,
under the largest suffering force, never in peacetime. Measuring what actually
happened rather than pass or fail found three real planner defects, each of which
would have shipped: it ignored foreign land claims, it took a company the arcane
survey had already spent, and it ignored the thirty-two-depot cap. All three are
the same mistake - planning from one snapshot without reconciling against the
rules or against its own earlier orders in the same pass.

Two earlier attempts at this were reverted on the conclusion that AI supply
awareness shifts campaign length out of band. That conclusion was wrong. The
pacing tests play a four-realm tiny map; the 350-400 turn target describes a
standard map with twelve realms. Measured under rules 29, with the AI playing
supply and no content change at all, the headline campaign runs 388 turns, inside
the target. The tiny proxies run 201, 290 and 296/464 across two epic seeds.
Sweeping the Epic project price to 44,000 and 52,000 overshot the headline to 411
and 440, so the pace content is untouched, the seal stays 015468d1, and the proxy
bounds are re-derived from measurement and labelled as proxies.

A genuine rules-28 campaign and its archive from e8cb13e load at turn 61, re-seal
to identical v28 bytes, replay exactly, round trip through a v29 envelope and
continue.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## You can see it now, and so can they

Supply has decided every campaign since it arrived, and until now you could not see it. The ground your hearths and depots can feed is drawn straight onto the map — a pale outline under everything else, on by default, and switchable off from the map guide if you would rather read it from the panels.

Depots can also be pulled down. When they arrived they came with upkeep and no way to stop paying it short of an enemy taking the post off you, which was simply a mistake. Stand a company on your own depot and you can dismantle it; the upkeep stops that moment and the ground it fed goes quiet again.

The larger change is that rival realms now play supply too. A realm at war whose army is wasting away outside its lines will stop and raise a depot under it rather than give up the campaign. It pays for it, it keeps paying for it, and you can go and pull it down.

That last part took three attempts, and the first two were abandoned on the belief that a competent AI made campaigns finish too quickly. That turned out to be a misreading of our own tests: the fast ones play a cramped four-realm map, while the length we actually aim for describes a full twelve-realm world. Measured properly, that campaign now runs 388 turns — right where it is meant to sit — with nothing about the game's balance changed to get there.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: docs: publish a journal note for supply depots
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: supply depots (rules/save 28)
body:
Supply followed hearths, and hearths came from founding or conquest. A realm
could reach further by building a road, but only across ground it already held,
and an army put ashore overseas had no way to be fed short of founding a town.
The one lever the system offered - take the next hearth - was the same lever the
system was meant to make expensive.

A company now spends its movement and forty coin to raise a depot where it
stands. The depot feeds two hexes of open country around it, or four along a
road: half a hearth's reach, seeded into the same search. It costs two coin a
turn, charged with every other obligation, so a network of them is a real line in
the budget rather than a free map. Depots of one realm keep three hexes between
them and a realm may hold thirty-two, so reach is a network of posts rather than
a carpet. And any enemy company that walks onto a depot razes it at the end of
the turn, telling both realms - so a supply network is now a thing to raid and a
thing to defend.

Refusals are plain, and the panel gives them in the same order the rules do: an
embarked army, a spent company, an empty purse, a hearth already on that ground,
a depot already there, a neighbour's claim, then the spacing rule.

Rules 28 adds state, not content, so the seal stays 015468d1. A genuine rules-27
campaign and its archive from b840150 load at turn 61, re-seal to identical v27
bytes, replay exactly, round trip through a v28 envelope and continue ten more
turns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## Somewhere to put the stores

Supply follows your hearths, which meant that until now the only way to reach further was to take someone else's — the very thing supply was supposed to make expensive. March an army into open country, or put one ashore on a coast you do not own, and there was nothing you could do about it except found a town.

Now a company can stop and raise a depot where it stands. Forty coin and the rest of its movement, and the ground two hexes around it is fed — four hexes along a road. That is half of what a hearth reaches, which is enough to carry an advance forward one bound at a time, and not enough to make distance stop mattering.

They are not free to keep. Each one draws two coin a turn alongside every other obligation, so a long chain of them is a real decision about what else you are not buying. They also stand apart — three hexes between any two of yours, thirty-two at most — so what you build is a line of posts rather than a blanket.

And they can be taken from you. Any enemy company that walks onto a depot pulls it down at the end of the turn, and both sides hear about it. A raiding party that slips behind your army and sits on the post it is eating from now does something that a battle cannot: it does not beat your army, it strands it.

So there are two ways to sustain a war now, and they cost different things. Take the next hearth, and it feeds you as it fed its old owner. Or build your own line forward, pay for it every turn, and keep something behind you worth guarding.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: docs: publish a journal note for supply lines
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: supply lines (rules/save 27)
body:
Distance cost nothing. An army twelve hexes inside an enemy realm fought as well
as one standing in its capital, rested as well, and could stay forever. Nothing
made a deep invasion harder than a shallow one.

Every hearth now feeds the ground around it: four hexes over open country, twice
as far along a built road. Supply is derived from the map every time it is asked,
so nothing is stored and the save shape is unchanged. An enemy company standing
on a hex stops supply passing through it, a foreign hearth blocks it, and a
hearth under siege feeds nobody - so raiding a supply line is now a real thing to
do, and taking a border town is what lets an invasion continue.

Each turn outside supply a company loses four strength, down to a fifth of its
full strength and no further, and recovers morale and fatigue at a third of the
ordinary rate: it falls behind a fed enemy rather than collapsing. Supply is the
price of massing a force, never a tax on exploring - a force of fewer than three
companies forages for itself, as does any expedition carrying a caravan, as does
every army of a realm that holds no hearth, which is every realm's opening.

Two first-cut rules were wrong and the campaign suite caught both. Attrition from
two companies starved colonising expeditions, so the AI founded one town instead
of many. Suppressing recovery entirely drove an unsupplied army's morale to one,
so attacks failed and no realm reached a victory inside its pacing window.

Rules 27 changes behaviour, not state or content, so the seal stays 015468d1. A
genuine rules-26 campaign and its archive from bb6fa8d load at turn 61, re-seal
to identical v26 bytes, replay exactly, round trip through a v27 envelope and
continue ten more turns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## Distance finally costs something

An army twelve hexes inside someone else's realm used to fight exactly as well as one standing in its own capital. It rested as well, it recovered as fast, and it could stay there forever. Nothing in the game made a deep invasion harder than a shallow one.

Hearths now feed the ground around them — four hexes over open country, and twice as far along a road you have built. That is your supply, and it moves with your hearths rather than your borders. Roads are no longer only about marching speed; they are how a realm reaches.

It can be cut. An enemy company standing on a hex stops supply passing through it. A hearth under siege feeds nobody at all. So there is now something to do with a fast company besides fight: get behind an enemy army and sit on the road it is eating from.

A force left outside supply loses four strength a turn — down to a fifth of its full strength, never further — and rests badly, recovering morale and fatigue at a third of the usual rate. It does not collapse. It simply falls behind an enemy that is being fed, which is what eventually decides the fight.

None of this is a tax on exploring. A force of fewer than three companies forages for itself, so scouts and raiding parties go where they like. So does any expedition carrying a caravan, so settling is never punished. And a realm that holds no hearth at all — every realm on turn one — has no line to cut in the first place.

The shape this gives a war is the point. You cannot simply march to someone's capital any more. You take the border hearth first, because a captured hearth feeds *you*, and then the next one. Your selected force will tell you which hearth is feeding it, or what standing outside is costing it, and anything starving is called out in the end-of-turn list under its own heading.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: docs: publish a journal note for grouped attention
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: group what wants a decision by cause
body:
The end-of-turn list reported two totals and offered one way through them: press
Next and read each entity's reason as it arrived. On a wide realm that said how
much work there was and nothing about what kind, and the only way to find three
interrupted routes among a hundred idle companies was to walk all hundred.

Every candidate now carries the cause that put it there - movement remaining, an
interrupted route, a stalled posting, an empty production queue, a stalled
charter or unassigned households - derived from the same observation its reason
already came from. The command bar lists one row per cause, largest first, and
each row is its own queue: clicking it jumps to the first entity of that cause
and the existing Next and Previous controls cycle within it.

This is a UI change over the existing read model. No command, no state, no rules
or save bump, and the content seal is untouched; totals, shortcuts, wrap-around
order and the spoken notice are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## What actually wants you

Two numbers at the bottom of the screen used to be the whole story: so many armies needing orders, so many idle settlements. They told you how much work was waiting and nothing at all about what kind, and the only way through was to press Next until you had seen all of it.

Now the list tells you its shape. **What wants a decision** breaks the totals into the reasons behind them, largest first — a hundred companies with movement remaining, forty hearths with an empty production queue, three companies with an interrupted route.

And each line is its own queue. Click the interrupted routes and you go straight to the first one; Next and Previous then walk only those three, not the hundred. Finding the handful of things that have actually gone wrong no longer means visiting everything that hasn't.

Between this and the hearth charters and army postings, a wide realm's end of turn is finally about exceptions. What answers for itself stays quiet; what is stuck says so, and says why.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: docs: publish a journal note for standing postings
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: standing postings and muster points (rules/save 26)
body:
An army may now be posted to a hex it has explored. Each turn it marches there
under the ordinary travel order - the same pathing, visibility and
hostile-sighting pause a player gets - and then holds the hex or joins the force
standing on it, merging the turn it arrives under the ordinary command capacity.
A posting only ever starts a march for an army that has no travel order of its
own, so an active route runs and a paused route keeps its reason; clearing it
returns the army to direct orders.

A hearth may also name a muster point. Every company it raises is posted there
the turn it forms and joins what it finds, which removes the singleton marching
and merging the production panel previously asked for by hand.

A posting always states where it stands - marching, standing, its paused route's
reason, no known route, nothing to join, or aboard a fleet - derived on demand
rather than stored, so nothing is stale in a save, a replay or the chronicle. An
army under a working posting leaves the next-action list and a stalled one
appears with the posting's own reason, so with rules 25's charters both halves
of a turn's busywork now answer for themselves.

Rules 26 adds state, not content, so the seal stays 015468d1. A genuine rules-25
campaign and its 2,181-order archive from a29ec80 load at turn 61, re-seal to
identical v25 bytes, replay exactly, round trip through a v26 envelope and
continue ten more turns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## Companies that know where to go

Raise a company and it used to arrive as its own little army, standing in the hearth that built it, waiting for you to walk it across the map and fold it into the force it was always meant to join. Six hearths raising troops meant six of those walks, every time.

Now an army can be posted. Name a hex it has explored and it marches there on its own, under exactly the travel order you would have given it — the same roads, the same fog, the same halt when something hostile comes into view. When it arrives it either holds the hex or joins the force standing on it, folding in the moment it gets there.

A posting never argues with you. It only moves an army that has no travel order of its own, so anything you order yourself happens first and the posting waits its turn. Clear it and the army is back under direct orders, with nothing to undo.

The part that saves the most clicking is the muster point. Give a hearth one, and every company it raises is posted there the turn it forms and joins whatever it finds. Set it once at the start of a war and the reinforcements simply arrive.

And a posting tells you where it stands: marching, standing, or stuck — and if it is stuck, why. There is no known route. There is nothing here to join. The road was interrupted. A posted army that is getting on with it drops out of your end-of-turn list entirely; a stuck one shows up with its reason attached. Between this and the hearth charters, what is left in that list is the things that actually want you.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: docs: publish a journal note for standing charters
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: standing hearth charters (rules/save 25)
body:
A hearth may now hold a standing charter instead of an order every turn. It
places one order whenever its queue is empty, so anything ordered by hand takes
precedence and simply delays it, and revoking returns the hearth to direct
orders. A charter never spends more than its ceiling on a single work, never
draws the treasury below forty coin, and is answered after upkeep is paid, so a
policy cannot starve a wage.

Works, Wealth and Learning finish the same hearth and differ only in what they
reach for first, with ties falling to the cheaper work; Muster raises the most
capable company the ceiling allows and never a caravan or a hull. Every order
goes through the ordinary production rules, and a hearth that changes hands ends
its charter rather than serving a conqueror. What a charter will do next - or
one of five plain refusals - is derived on demand rather than stored, so no
explanation is ever stale in a save, a replay or the chronicle.

A hearth under a working charter leaves the next-action list entirely, and a
stalled one appears with the charter's own reason in place of the generic empty
queue notice. The AI leaves a Works charter on hearths one turn's orders could
not reach, and never charters Muster.

Adding a schema to save.ts exposed a real import cycle: save.ts took MAX_EVENTS
from simulation.ts while simulation.ts took MAX_FACTIONS back, and MAX_EVENTS
bounds a schema built at module scope, so any entry point reaching simulation
first left that bound undefined. MAX_EVENTS now lives beside MAX_FACTIONS.

Rules 25 adds state, not content, so the seal stays 015468d1. A genuine rules-24
campaign and its 2,589-order archive from 0fd242a load at turn 61, re-seal to
identical v24 bytes, replay exactly, round trip through a v25 envelope and
continue ten more turns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## A hearth that answers for itself

The bigger your realm got, the longer your turn took. Forty hearths meant forty visits, most of them to say the same thing again. That is the wrong way round, and it is what standing charters are for.

Give a hearth a charter and it places its own order whenever its queue runs empty. You set two things: what it reaches for first — Works, Wealth, Learning or Muster — and the most coin it may spend on any single order. It never spends past that ceiling, it always leaves forty coin in the treasury, and it waits until wages are paid before it buys anything.

A charter is not an autopilot you have to fight. It only acts on an empty queue, so anything you order by hand simply comes first and the charter waits. Revoke it and the hearth is back under direct orders, with nothing to undo.

It also tells you what it is about to do. The panel names the next work — *Next: Charter market* — or gives you the reason there isn't one: every building already stands there, the ceiling is too low, the treasury is near its reserve. That reason now replaces the generic nag in your next-action list, and a hearth whose charter is working drops out of that list altogether. What is left is the hearths that actually want a decision from you.

Rival realms use the same mechanism: when a realm grows wider than one turn of orders can cover, the hearths its planner never reached keep building on a charter of their own.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: docs: publish a journal note for unbinding
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: unbinding and culture traditions (rules/save 24)
body:
Unbinding answers a working with a working. It strips the binding from one
active enemy formation - any ward is undone - and every Waykeeper escorting
that formation loses the coming round. It costs five strain and may be used
once a battle, so a counter is a decision rather than a reflex, and a formation
carrying neither a ward nor a caster is refused with a reason. The interruption
is ordinary saved state, so it survives a save, a replay and the chronicle.

Cultures now train their own tradition. A Waykeeper takes the aptitudes of the
culture that appoints them: the Cinder March and Emberwake Convocation reach
the second degree of Flame, the Sepulchral Synod and Margin Observance the
second degree of Rune - and only the second degree of Rune can unbind. Every
other culture keeps the common training and cannot counter at all. A discovery
inside a realm's own tradition is studied at three quarters of its price, so
access and cost both depend on who you are.

Magic content is versioned inside the content seal the way the pace table
already was: a pack is sealed with the workings that campaign could reach.
Every frozen pack still reproduces exactly, and a genuine rules-23 save and its
1,944-order archive from ef7a831 load, re-seal to identical bytes, replay
exactly and continue.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## An answer to a working

Until now a working could only be met with steel. Unbinding changes that. It is cast at one enemy formation on the field and strips the binding from it: any ward is undone, and every Waykeeper riding with that formation is jarred badly enough to lose the coming round. It costs five strain and can be used once in a battle, so it is a decision about when the other side has committed, not something to lead with.

It also needs something to undo. Aimed at a formation that carries neither a ward nor a caster, Unbinding refuses and tells you why — *nothing binds this formation* — rather than burning the one use you had.

The bigger change is who can cast it. A Waykeeper now trains in the tradition of the culture that appointed them. The Cinder March and the Emberwake Convocation reach the second degree of Flame; the Sepulchral Synod and the Margin Observance reach the second degree of Rune. Only the second degree of Rune can unbind, so two realms in the world can answer a working and the rest cannot — they have to beat it another way. A realm also studies theory inside its own tradition at three quarters of the usual price, so what your culture is good at is cheaper as well as reachable.

Automatic casting plays the same board: a counter goes to the strongest binding on the field, a ward to the front rank, and a damaging working to whichever enemy is nearest to breaking.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: docs: publish a journal note for arcane seams
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: arcane seams and site-gated Arcane Theory (rules/save 23)
body:
The Ashfall left arcane seams under Ashfall-glass ground. Where a seam lies is
derived from the world's seed like any other natural feature, so a save records
only which realms have paid to survey them: a standard map hides fourteen seams
among a hundred and sixty-two visible glass hexes, a tiny map three among
twenty-three.

Any company may spend its movement and 24 coin to survey the ground it stands
on, revealing seams within two hexes to that realm alone. An empty survey says
so and still costs. A surveyed seam inside a realm's borders draws two ashglass
a turn beside the hearth's ordinary yield and falls with that hearth.

Arcane Theory now needs such a seam, so magic begins with geography a realm
must find, take and keep. Until now ashglass - the one arcane-tagged resource -
had no magical consumer at all, and research was gated only by an archive and
accumulated knowledge.

A realm holding no seam surveys its own hinterland from surplus at most once
every six turns, prefers a surveyed seam when its borders grow, and never
marches a surveying company away in the same turn. The selected company offers
a survey with its price and its refusal reason; the Arcane Theory tab lists the
seams the realm has surveyed and whether each is held.

Measured: a standard twelve-realm campaign with eight city-states ends on turn
231, six realms surveyed and held a seam, and one completed Arcane Theory
through it. A genuine rules-22 save and its 1,993-order archive from 6644f80
load, re-seal to identical bytes, replay exactly and continue.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## What the Ashfall left behind

Magic now begins with ground. The Ashfall left arcane seams buried under the vitrified glass it scattered, and where those seams lie is a property of the world itself — the same for every realm that plays it, and hidden from all of them until someone goes looking.

Any company can stop and survey the ground it stands on for twenty-four coin. The survey spends that company's movement and reveals any seam within two hexes, to your realm alone; a survey that finds nothing says so and still costs. Ashfall glass is visible to everyone, so you can see where it is worth looking without being told where the seams are.

A seam inside your borders draws ashglass every turn, and falls to whoever takes the hearth that holds it. And a held seam is now what allows a realm to study Arcane Theory at all: research alone no longer reaches magic. You have to find the ground, take it, and keep it.

Rival realms do the same. A realm holding no seam will survey its own hinterland from time to time, and will reach for a seam it has found when its borders grow.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: test: prove the campaign-safety scenarios under the rules that ship
body:
The campaign-safety findings were corrected and reviewed under rules 17, and
rules 18-22 have since changed pacing, sieges, seats and diplomacy. An audit of
all nine findings shows eight already run at current rules with ordinary
commands; the pending-assault regression did not, because it built its
garrison, siege and turn at rules 17 only, so the food-store siege model never
touched it. It now builds its scenario under the rules being checked and proves
the same invariant at rules 17 and at the shipping rules. The remaining rule-16
cases stay pinned on purpose: they are captured evidence that old envelopes
still refuse what they refused.

The retained set - ten files, 66 checks - passes and no finding re-opened. The
roadmap item now asks that each scenario keep running against the rules that
ship rather than the rules it was first closed under.

Patronage also gains its browser coverage: offering an oath discloses the whole
bargain before it is sent, and an accepted oath is visible to both realms,
refuses war, survives a save and can be released.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: docs: publish a journal note for client states
body: Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: client states and negotiated unification (rules/save 22)
body:
A realm may now take another realm as its client: a subsidy paid on
acceptance, tribute every turn for an agreed term, and no war between patron
and client while the oath holds. The client keeps its own hearths, armies and
orders — patronage is an obligation between realms, not a conquest. Every
term is disclosed before consent, and an offer that can no longer be funded
says so rather than failing on acceptance.

A patron may release a client. A client may renounce: lawfully once the term
has run, or as a breach that ends the binding peace between them and is
remembered as a grievance. A client that cannot pay for three turns running
falls out of its obligation. Patronage may not chain, cycle, duplicate or
cross an active war.

A client's hearths stand behind its patron's unification bid, so the second
victory path is now reachable through diplomacy as well as conquest, and the
Victory tab separates hearths held from hearths pledged. The AI courts weaker
neighbours — city-states first — at most once every ten turns, weighs an offer
against its own hearths, income and wars, and never plans a war on its own
patron or client.

Patronage keeps patrons and clients out of each other's wars, which lengthened
the longest campaigns, so Long is now 32,000 and Epic 36,000: a standard
twelve-realm map ends on turn 205, 283 and 342 for Standard, Long and Epic.
The rules-21 pack is frozen as f70d99d5; a genuine rules-21 save and its
2,037-order archive from cce82cf load, re-seal to identical bytes, replay
exactly and continue.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## Oaths between realms

A realm can now take another realm as its client. The patron pays a subsidy when the oath is accepted; the client pays tribute every turn for an agreed term, keeps its own hearths, armies and orders, and neither realm may make war on the other while the obligation holds. Every term — what is paid now, what is owed each turn, how long it binds, and what it forbids — is stated before either side consents.

The oath can end three ways. A patron may release its client at any time. A client may walk away lawfully once the term has run. Or it may renounce early, which is a breach: the binding peace between the two realms ends and the broken word is remembered.

This changes how a campaign can be won. A client's hearths stand behind its patron's unification bid, so the second victory path is now open to diplomacy as well as conquest — and city-states, who have no wars of their own to fight, make willing clients. Rival realms court them, and the Victory tab shows how many hearths are your own and how many were pledged to you.

Because patrons and clients keep out of each other's wars, campaigns ran longer than intended, so the two longest paces are re-priced from measured games. Saved campaigns from the previous rules load unchanged and replay exactly.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: city-states, wider realms and 42-realm maps (rules/save 21)
body:
Twenty-four chartered city-states now settle the land between realms. Each
borrows one culture's art and unit roster while keeping its own name, banner
colour, motto and lore; it holds a single hearth, opens no war and pursues no
victory, but builds, defends, holds territory and makes peace through the
ordinary commands. Their lore is a new book in the site's library.

Realms also run wider: founding costs less as a realm grows, civic borders
grow in a handful of turns instead of dozens, and administration and territory
upkeep are gentler. Seats past the authored roster take their own epithet and
colour, and the renderer washes their borrowed art in that colour, so a
crowded map never shows two identical banners. Campaigns seat up to 42 realms
plus their city-states, and Unification now needs two thirds of the world's
hearths.

Also fixes a growth panel that quoted rules-16 founding and upkeep prices
while the turn charged rules-21 prices, and an AI that could reserve more coin
for its victory project than it actually had free, cancelling the caravan and
hull it had already protected.

Measured: the standard map with 12 realms and 8 city-states ends on turn 199
(Standard), 303 (Long) and 447 (Epic); 42 realms and 12 city-states claim 88%
of its land by turn 193. A genuine rules-20 save and its 1,192-order archive
from c7089f1 load, re-seal to identical bytes, replay exactly and continue.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
notes:
## City-states and wider realms

Twenty-four city-states now hold the land between the great realms. Each is one settlement that never joined anything: it borrows a neighbouring culture's art, crafts and troops, and keeps only its own name, banner colour, motto and the particular bargain it refuses to sign. A city-state founds nothing further, opens no war and pursues no victory, but it builds, defends its hearth, holds territory and answers envoys like any other power. Their register and histories are published in the lore library.

Realms also run wider. Planting a hearth costs less as a realm grows, civic borders fill in a handful of turns instead of dozens, and administration and territory upkeep are gentler, so a campaign ends with far more of the map settled. A world can now seat up to forty-two realms alongside its city-states; seats past the authored cultures take their own epithet and banner colour, and their borrowed artwork is washed in it, so no two banners on a crowded map look alike.

Saved campaigns from the previous rules load unchanged, keep their exact bytes and replay from their archives.

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: sieges eat stored food (rules/save 20)
body:
Siege supplies now count the whole turns a blockaded town's actual food store
lasts (its food yield is cut off while it keeps eating); an empty store starves
the militia's morale each turn. Well-fed towns hold out longer, so attackers
choose between an early assault and starving the garrison. The siege panel
shows food stores in turns. Historical rules keep the fixed three-turn count.

Genuine rules-19 saves and archives load, re-seal identically, replay and
continue. Pacing stays within target (Standard/12: 207/267/316 turns).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: Unification victory (rules/save 19)
body:
A realm holding more than half of the world's hearths (at least six) opens a
public Unification bid at its capital; holding the majority and that capital
through the pace's response window wins. Losing either ends the bid. The
Victory tab shows progress and blockers; chronicle and banner name the path.

Rules 18 content (98b97bba) is frozen: genuine rules-18 saves and archives load,
re-seal identically, replay and continue. Historical rules never open bids.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ErikBurdett
subject: feat: generator 8 Civilization-style maps, 12-realm defaults and build-only CI
body:
- Generator 8: slightly smaller maps (Standard 224x140 for 12 realms, Tiny
  48x32 through 352x220) and seven map types: Continents, Pangaea, Fractal,
  Islands, Archipelago, Earth-like (latitude climate) and Inland Sea.
  Generators 1-7 remain byte-identical (historical seal tests).
- Rules 18 accepts generator-8 worlds; older rules default to generator 7 and
  refuse generator-8 geography. The new-campaign form offers Map type,
  defaults to Standard/12 and states each pace's target length.
- AI: at peace, newly unlocked roles wait until expansion is funded, so no
  culture starves its next caravan.
- Tests: mapgen suite 30 s -> 6 s; seed-specific scenarios pin generator 7;
  full local suite 1,793 tests in ~27 s.
- CI: Verify typechecks and builds; Pages typechecks, builds and deploys.
  Unit, campaign and browser testing stays local.

notes:
## Dispatches launch

This change introduced the public developer journal: three illustrated, source-linked dispatches covering campaign safety, archive durability, and the twenty-four-culture baseline. It included searchable archive controls, stable dispatch query links, a scope ledger, source library and contributor guidance.

The journal reused retained Hearth & Card materials and four provenance-recorded game screenshots. It introduced no game rules or new game artwork; it is a development-demo publication, not 1.0 acceptance.
